label: What is your company's full legal name?
description: This name is printed on every invoice, order and report. Enter it exactly as on your incorporation or GST certificate. A name that does not match your registration causes problems with customers' accounts teams and tax filings.

label: Which country is your company registered in?
description: This loads the right chart of accounts, currency and tax set-up. Choose the country where you pay tax. A wrong country loads the wrong accounts, which then have to be undone by hand.

label: What is your company's PAN?
description: This is your main tax identity and appears on documents that need it. Enter the ten-character PAN. A missing or wrong PAN leads to rejected TDS returns and problems when customers deduct tax from your payments.

label: What is the first line of your registered address?
description: This is printed on invoices and used for e-way bills. Enter it exactly as on your GST certificate. An address that differs from your registration can make customers' tax credits harder to claim.

label: Which city or town is it in?
description: This completes your printed address. Enter the city as on official papers. Spelling it differently in different places makes location reports unreliable.

label: Which state is it in?
description: The state decides whether a sale is taxed as local or inter-state GST. Enter the state where you are registered for GST. A wrong state charges the wrong tax on every invoice.

label: What is the PIN code?
description: This is needed for e-way bills and distance calculation. Enter the six-digit PIN code. A wrong code makes e-way bills fail or show the wrong distance.

label: What is the GSTIN for this address?
description: This is printed on invoices and used in GST returns and e-invoices. Enter the 15-character number from your GST certificate. Leave it blank only if this site is not registered for GST.

label: What type of GST registration do you have?
description: This decides how tax is worked out and reported. Most businesses are Registered Regular. A wrong category, such as Composition instead of Regular, files tax incorrectly on every invoice.
options:
Registered Regular
Registered Composition
Unregistered
SEZ
Overseas
Deemed Export
UIN Holders
Tax Deductor
Tax Collector
Input Service Distributor

label: Which day of the week are you closed?
description: This day is marked as a holiday every week for attendance, planning and delivery dates. Most Indian businesses choose Sunday. Getting it wrong spoils attendance, payroll and production schedules.
options:
Sunday
Monday
Tuesday
Wednesday
Thursday
Friday
Saturday

label: Should item code and description be combined into one column on printed documents?
description: Compact printing saves space on long invoices. Businesses with long item lists usually say yes. The wrong choice either wastes paper or squeezes details customers need to read.

label: On what date does your financial year start?
description: This sets where yearly profit and loss begins; the end date and year name are worked out for you. Almost every Indian business starts on 1 April. A wrong date means annual figures will not match your tax return.

label: Which bank do you mainly use for business?
description: This lets payments and statements be matched to the right bank. Add your main current account first. Without it, payments cannot be reconciled.

label: What is your bank account number?
description: This is printed on invoices so customers know where to pay. Enter it exactly as on your cheque book. A single wrong digit sends payments to the wrong place.

label: What is the IFSC code of your branch?
description: Customers need this to pay you by NEFT or RTGS. It is the eleven-character code on your cheque book. A wrong code makes transfers fail.

label: What do you call your usual credit arrangement with customers?
description: This names the rule used to work out when an invoice is due. Most businesses use a label such as Net 30. A clear name makes it easy to pick the right terms on each invoice.

label: How many days after the invoice do customers normally pay?
description: This sets due dates and drives overdue reports. Most Indian businesses give 30 or 45 days. Too long hides late payers; too short makes everyone look overdue.

label: Which payment terms should new customers get by default?
description: These terms fill in on invoices unless a customer has their own. Choose your usual credit terms. Left blank, every invoice falls due immediately.

label: What is the most a customer may owe you before new orders are stopped?
description: This is the default limit for customers with none of their own; zero means no limit. Many businesses use about two months of a typical customer's purchases. Too low blocks genuine orders; too high lets bad debts build up.

label: Who may approve an order for a customer who is over their credit limit?
description: People with this role can go past a credit limit; everyone else is stopped. Most businesses give it to the accounts manager only. Left blank, nobody can release a held order.

label: By what percentage may an invoice exceed the order amount?
description: This stops staff invoicing more than was agreed. Most businesses set zero or a small figure for rounding. Too high lets overcharging go unnoticed.

label: Who may invoice beyond that allowance?
description: People with this role can bill more than the order when there is a genuine reason. Most businesses give it to the accounts manager. Without anyone, legitimate extra billing cannot be booked.

label: Should the system stop the same supplier bill number being entered twice?
description: This guards against paying a supplier twice for one bill. Most businesses say yes. Without it, a duplicate bill can go unnoticed until the supplier is overpaid.

label: When an invoice is cancelled, should its payment be freed up automatically?
description: If yes, the payment is released so it can be matched to another invoice. Most businesses say yes. If no, every correction needs the payment unlinked by hand first.

label: Should invoices copy the payment terms from the order automatically?
description: If yes, due dates agreed on the order carry through to the invoice. Businesses that agree terms per order say yes. If no, agreed credit periods get lost at invoicing.

label: Should GST be decided by the billing address or the shipping address?
description: This picks which customer address decides local or inter-state tax. Most businesses use the shipping address, the place of supply for goods. The wrong choice charges IGST where CGST and SGST were due, or the reverse.

label: Should advances from customers and to suppliers be kept in their own accounts?
description: If yes, money received or paid before an invoice sits in a separate advance account until matched. Businesses taking many advances say yes. If no, advances mix into party balances and are harder to track for GST.

label: Should invoice totals be left unrounded, without rounding to the nearest rupee?
description: Most Indian businesses round totals to the rupee and say no. Say yes only if customers need exact paise totals. Changing it later makes old and new invoices total differently.

label: Which branch, plant or division do you want to see profit for separately?
description: Each name becomes a cost centre that income and costs can be charged to. Single-site businesses leave this blank. Too many make reports hard to read and entries easy to misfile.

label: Do you need e-way bills for goods you move?
description: If yes, e-way bills can be created from invoices and delivery notes. Businesses moving goods worth over Rs 50,000 per consignment say yes. If no, e-way bills must be made separately on the portal.

label: Is your turnover above the e-invoicing limit?
description: If yes, B2B invoices get an IRN and QR code from the government portal. Businesses over the current turnover limit must say yes. Issuing B2B invoices without e-invoicing when it applies makes them invalid for the buyer's input credit.

label: From what date does e-invoicing apply to you?
description: Invoices dated on or after this day need an e-invoice. Enter the date your turnover first crossed the limit, or your go-live date. A wrong date leaves some invoices without IRN or asks for IRN on old ones.

label: Do you sell any goods or services where the buyer pays the GST?
description: If yes, reverse charge can be marked on sales invoices. Goods transport agencies and some service providers say yes. If no, such invoices charge GST that the customer should have paid.

label: Do you export, import or supply to SEZ units?
description: If yes, export, import and SEZ invoices and bills of entry are set up. Exporters, importers and SEZ suppliers say yes. If no, these transactions cannot be recorded with the right GST treatment.

label: Is there a group of sales taxed differently, such as exports or SEZ?
description: Each answer becomes a tax category so the right tax is picked for those customers automatically. Exporters and SEZ suppliers usually add one. Without it, staff change taxes by hand and errors follow.

label: Where else do you keep stock, besides your main store?
description: Each location becomes a warehouse so stock can be counted and moved between them. Name it after the area or building; leave blank if you have only one. Names that are too alike lead to stock booked to the wrong place.

label: Where do you keep goods that fail inspection or come back faulty?
description: A separate location keeps rejected goods out of saleable stock. Businesses that inspect incoming material usually create one. Without it, faulty goods count as available and may be sold by mistake.

label: Will you give each item your own code, or let the system number them?
description: This decides how new items are identified. Businesses with existing product codes choose Item Code. Mixing approaches later makes the item list hard to search.

label: How should the cost of stock be worked out?
description: FIFO assumes the oldest stock is used first; Moving Average blends all purchase prices. Most Indian businesses choose FIFO. It cannot be changed for an item once it has transactions.

label: May staff dispatch goods the system shows as out of stock?
description: If yes, deliveries go ahead even when recorded stock is too low. Most businesses say no to keep stock figures honest. Saying yes hides missing receipts and gives wrong stock values.

label: By what percentage may you deliver or receive more than was ordered?
description: This allows small excesses, such as a supplier sending a few extra kilos. Businesses dealing by weight or length often allow 2 to 5 per cent. Too high lets large unordered quantities slip in.

label: Who may approve receiving or delivering beyond that allowance?
description: People with this role can go past the allowance when there is a genuine reason. Most businesses give it to the store or purchase manager. Without anyone, legitimate excess deliveries cannot be booked.

label: Should purchase requests be raised automatically when stock falls below its reorder level?
description: If yes, material requests are created for items below the levels set on them. Businesses with regular raw material use say yes. If no, someone must watch stock by hand and shortages are missed.

label: Do you need to set stock aside for particular customer orders?
description: If yes, stock can be reserved against a sales order so nobody else uses it. Businesses holding goods for confirmed orders say yes. Without it, reserved goods can go to another customer.

label: Should a price typed on a transaction be saved to the price list when the item has none?
description: If yes, the first rate used for an item is stored for next time. Businesses building their price lists as they go say yes. If no, prices must be entered into the price list separately.

label: Do you scan barcodes when entering stock or sales?
description: If yes, a barcode field appears on stock and sales forms for scanning. Shops and warehouses with labelled goods say yes. If no, items must be picked from a list by hand.

label: What do you call the checklist used to inspect your main material?
description: A template holds the list of checks so inspectors fill in the same points each time. Name it after the material; leave blank if you do not inspect. Without templates, inspections are inconsistent.

label: If an inspection is not completed, should the receipt or delivery be stopped or just warned?
description: Stop blocks the transaction until inspection is finished; Warn lets it through with a message. Businesses where quality is critical choose Stop. Warn is easily ignored, so uninspected goods slip through.

label: If goods fail inspection, should the receipt or delivery be stopped or just warned?
description: Stop blocks rejected goods from being booked as accepted; Warn only shows a message. Most businesses that inspect choose Stop. Warn lets failed goods enter saleable stock.

label: What is a main category of products you sell or buy?
description: Products, Raw Material, Services and Consumable already exist; add categories that match your range. Most businesses add a handful. Too many clutter reports.

label: Do you have another set of selling prices, such as wholesale? What is it called?
description: One selling and one buying price list already exist. Add another only for a separate rate card; leave blank otherwise. Without it, staff must remember special rates and get some wrong.

label: What type of customer do you have that is not Commercial, Individual, Government or Non Profit?
description: Those four groups already exist; add your own to report sales by customer type. Distributors and dealers are common additions. Without suitable groups you cannot see which customers are most profitable.

label: Which region or state do you sell into most?
description: Territories let you see sales by area and set targets. Most Indian businesses add the states or zones they cover. Leaving everyone in one territory makes regional reports impossible.

label: Who is one of your salespeople?
description: Salespeople are credited on orders so you can track their sales and commission. Add each person in your sales team. Without them you cannot see who brought in which business.

label: What commission percentage does this salesperson earn?
description: This is used to work out commission on their sales. Many businesses pay 1 to 5 per cent; enter zero if none. A wrong figure leads to overpayment or disputes.

label: Should customers be identified by their name or by a customer code?
description: Customer Name is simplest; Naming Series gives each customer a running code. Businesses with many similar names choose Naming Series. Changing later leaves a mixed customer list.
options:
Customer Name
Naming Series
Auto Name

label: Which customer group should new customers go into by default?
description: This fills in on every new customer. Choose the group most of your customers belong to. A poor default means customers are misfiled unless staff correct each one.

label: Which territory should new customers go into by default?
description: This fills in on every new customer. Choose the area where most customers are. A poor default puts customers in the wrong region in reports.

label: Must every sale start with a sales order?
description: If yes, invoices and deliveries can only be made against an order. Make-to-order businesses say yes; counter sales say no. Saying yes for counter sales slows every sale.

label: Must goods be dispatched before they can be invoiced?
description: If yes, every invoice must follow a delivery note. Businesses that dispatch separately from billing say yes. Saying no then lets stock and invoices drift apart.

label: May sales staff change list prices on an order?
description: If no, staff must use the price list and show discounts separately. Most businesses say no. Saying yes lets prices be cut with no record of the discount.

label: Should the system stop sales below the item's purchase cost?
description: If yes, an order or invoice priced below cost is blocked. Most businesses say yes. If no, loss-making sales can go through unnoticed.

label: Must the invoice price match the order price exactly?
description: If yes, the rate cannot change between order and invoice. Businesses with agreed contract prices say yes. If no, prices can be altered at invoicing without anyone noticing.

label: May the same item appear more than once on one order?
description: If yes, an item can be listed on several lines, for example with different delivery dates. Businesses with staggered deliveries say yes. If no, such orders must be split.

label: May a customer's purchase order number be used on more than one sales order?
description: If yes, one customer PO can be split across several sales orders. Suppliers on rate contracts often say yes. If no, repeat use is blocked to stop orders being entered twice.

label: What is a main type of supplier you buy from?
description: Supplier groups let you see spending by type of supplier. Most businesses group by what they buy. Without groups, purchase reports are one long list.

label: Should suppliers be identified by their name or by a supplier code?
description: Supplier Name is simplest; Naming Series gives each supplier a running code. Businesses with codes already in use choose Naming Series. Changing later leaves a confusing list.
options:
Supplier Name
Naming Series
Auto Name

label: Which supplier group should new suppliers go into by default?
description: This fills in on every new supplier. Choose the group most suppliers belong to. A poor default misfiles suppliers unless corrected.

label: Must every purchase have an approved purchase order?
description: If yes, bills and receipts can only be entered against an order. Businesses wanting control over spending say yes. Saying no lets purchases happen without approval.

label: Must goods be received before the supplier's bill is entered?
description: If yes, you can only book a bill for goods that have arrived. Most stock-holding businesses say yes. Saying no risks paying for goods never received.

label: Must the supplier's bill match the purchase order price exactly?
description: If yes, a bill at a different rate from the order is blocked. Businesses with fixed supplier prices say yes. If no, price increases can be paid without approval.

label: May the same item appear more than once on one purchase order?
description: If yes, an item can be listed on several lines for staggered deliveries. Businesses ordering in instalments say yes. If no, such orders must be split.

label: Does your supplier still bill you for goods you reject on arrival?
description: If yes, rejected quantities are included in the bill and handled through a return. Most businesses say no. A wrong answer means bills that do not match what the supplier charged.

label: Where else do enquiries come from, beyond walk-ins, references, adverts, exhibitions and cold calls?
description: Common sources already exist; add others to see which bring the most business. Online marketplaces are typical additions. Without accurate sources you cannot tell where marketing money works best.

label: May the same email address be entered as more than one enquiry?
description: If no, the system warns when someone already recorded enquires again. Most businesses say no. Saying yes leads to duplicate records and two salespeople chasing one person.

label: Should a contact be created automatically for every new enquiry?
description: If yes, each lead's name, phone and email are saved as a contact straight away. Most businesses say yes. If no, contact details must be re-entered when the lead becomes a customer.

label: For how many days are your quotations normally valid?
description: This fills in the expiry date on new quotations. Most businesses quote for 15 or 30 days. Too long commits you to old prices after costs rise.

label: After how many days without a reply should an open opportunity be closed?
description: Answered but unfollowed opportunities close after this many days. Many businesses choose 15 to 30. Too short closes live deals; too long fills the pipeline with dead ones.

label: Should materials used be taken from the recipe or from what was actually sent to the floor?
description: BOM deducts standard quantities; Material Transferred deducts what was actually issued. Businesses with variable wastage choose Material Transferred. The wrong choice makes product costs and stock drift from reality.

label: Where are materials held while being worked on?
description: Materials issued to production sit here until finished. Most businesses use the Work In Progress location already created. A wrong choice mixes half-made goods with ready stock.

label: Where do finished products go once they are made?
description: Completed production is booked into this location. Most businesses use the Finished Goods location already created. A wrong choice means finished stock cannot be found for dispatch.

label: Do you record material used during production, not just at the end?
description: If yes, consumption can be booked in stages while a job runs. Long-running or process jobs say yes. If no, work-in-progress values are wrong until the job finishes.

label: By what percentage may planned production exceed what customers ordered?
description: This allows making a little extra beyond the sales order. Businesses expecting rejections allow 5 to 10 per cent. Too high ties up cash in unsold stock.

label: By what percentage may actual output exceed the work order quantity?
description: This lets the floor book slightly more finished goods than planned. Many businesses allow 0 to 5 per cent. Too high hides overuse of material.

label: Should batch or serial numbers for finished goods be created from the work order?
description: If yes, numbers are generated when production is planned so labels can be printed early. Businesses labelling on the line say yes. If no, numbers are created by hand when goods are finished.

label: Should product cost sheets update automatically when material prices change?
description: If yes, each bill of materials is re-costed from the latest prices. Businesses with volatile raw material prices say yes. If no, quotations may use old, too-low costs.

label: For job work, should material used be taken from the recipe or from what you sent the job worker?
description: BOM deducts standard quantities; Material Transferred deducts what was actually sent. Most businesses using job workers choose Material Transferred. The wrong choice leaves material at the job worker unaccounted for.

label: Should automatic planning of machine time be switched off?
description: If no, operations are scheduled on machines according to their working hours. Simple workshops without accurate operation times say yes. Planning without accurate times produces unrealistic schedules.

label: How many days ahead should machine time be planned?
description: Jobs are scheduled only within this window. Most businesses plan 30 days ahead. Too short makes longer jobs fail to schedule.

label: May jobs be scheduled beyond normal working hours?
description: If yes, operations can run past a machine's working hours. Businesses running regular overtime say yes. If no, jobs that do not fit a shift move to the next day.

label: Do you ever run production on holidays?
description: If yes, jobs may be scheduled on holidays. Continuous-process plants say yes. If no, planned dates skip holidays even when the plant runs.

label: What is one of your main machines or production lines?
description: Workstations are where operations happen and carry the running cost used in product costing. Add each key machine or line. Leaving them out removes machine and labour cost from product costs.

label: What does an hour on this machine cost you?
description: This hourly figure is added to the cost of every job run here — labour, power and the share of rent the machine takes. Work it out from what the machine and its operators cost in a month, divided by the hours it runs. A wrong figure makes products look more or less profitable than they are.

label: Should recorded hours be pulled into the customer's invoice automatically?
description: If yes, a project's timesheets can be added to its invoice in one step. Businesses billing by the hour say yes. If no, hours are copied by hand and some get missed.

label: May one person record time on two jobs at the same moment?
description: If no, overlapping timesheets for the same employee are blocked. Most businesses say no. Saying yes allows the same hours to be billed twice.
